facts.title: What the Real spacecraft scenario is
facts.text: Astro Pilot's Real spacecraft scenario is a rendezvous-and-docking simulation: a classical guidance, navigation and control (GNC) autopilot flies a 95-tonne Shuttle-class orbiter from about 2 km behind a Mir-class space station to a soft dock. It models the flight the way NASA plans proximity operations, instead of the game's asteroid-belt dodging.

facts.title: Why the real spacecraft docks, not dodges
facts.text: Real reaction-control jets give a Shuttle-class ship only about 0.08 m/s² of acceleration, but dodging Astro Pilot's asteroid belt would need about 35 g with 1.5–3.6 s of warning. So the Real spacecraft scenario does what real ships do: it does not dodge, it rendezvouses and docks.

facts.title: What GNC means in the docking autopilot
facts.text: GNC stands for guidance, navigation and control. In Astro Pilot's docking autopilot, navigation estimates position and velocity from simulated lidar, guidance picks the target velocity for the current phase once a second (1 Hz), and control fires the 22 jets ten times a second (10 Hz) to follow it. It is hand-designed classical GNC, not a trained neural network.

facts.title: Docking RL pilot is only planned
facts.text: A reinforcement-learning pilot for the docking scenario exists only in the design: a PPO 'residual' that would nudge the GNC velocity command by at most 0.05 m/s. It could ship only after matching GNC's captures with zero failures, staying within 5 % of its Δv and time, and improving collision avoidance. It is not installed; the classical GNC autopilot flies every docking run.

facts.title: Docking mission phases
facts.text: A full docking mission in Astro Pilot runs through the phases TRANSFER, H1 ACQ, H1, CORRIDOR, H2 and FINAL, ending in CAPTURE. BREAKOUT, the abort, can interrupt any phase. The HUD shows all of them as phase chips at the top left and highlights the current one.

facts.title: How long a docking mission takes
facts.text: A far-start docking mission lasts about 6,673 s of simulated time, roughly 111 minutes or 1.2 orbits: a 46-minute transfer, 23 minutes of H1 acquisition, a 5-minute hold, about 31 minutes in the corridor, a 1-minute hold at H2 and a 286 s final approach. With auto warp it plays in about 2.5 minutes on screen.

facts.title: Why the ship dips below to catch up
facts.text: In orbit a lower orbit is faster, so a ship below the station drifts forward relative to it and a ship above drifts backward. Astro Pilot's docking transfer uses this: it dips the ship about 437 m below the station so it gains 1,750 m in half an orbit, instead of simply thrusting toward the station.

facts.title: How the transfer is planned
facts.text: Astro Pilot's docking transfer is planned before departure: the nominal half-orbit hop flies if it passes the passive-safety check; otherwise the planner searches transfer times of 0.35–0.6 orbit and cross-track changes up to ±0.2 m/s for the cheapest passing plan. Two mid-course corrections, at one third and two thirds of the transfer, re-aim at H1 unless under 5 mm/s or unsafe.

facts.title: Cross-track offset keeps the transfer safe
facts.text: A far docking start begins about 250 m to the side of the station's orbital plane, at the edge of a free cross-track oscillation. This sideways separation keeps the transfer passively safe under drag: in the design analysis the worst 24-hour approach after the hop is about 250 m, but only 16.8 m without it.

facts.title: H1 ACQ: acquiring the first hold
facts.text: H1 ACQ (H1 acquisition) follows the docking transfer: the ship holds its along-track and radial position within ±3 m of the H1 point while its sideways offset swings naturally to zero over a quarter orbit, about 1,392 s. facts.title: H1: the first hold point
facts.text: H1 is the first docking hold point, 250 m behind the station's centre on V-bar, about 217 m between the docking ports. The autopilot keeps the ship in a ±3 m box there for at least 300 s, then checks GO before entering the approach corridor. The start=near flag begins a run at H1.

facts.title: GO criteria at the hold points
facts.text: GO at a docking hold (H1 or H2) requires attitude error under 2°, body rate under 0.1°/s, valid navigation, at least 40 % of the propellant left, an available passively safe breakout, and the ship at rest (under 1 cm/s) inside its hold box. After 1,800 s of NO-GO the autopilot breaks out.

facts.title: CORRIDOR: the V-bar approach speed
facts.text: In the CORRIDOR phase the docking ship closes along V-bar from H1 toward H2 at 0.1 % of the remaining port-to-port distance per second, clamped between 0.07 and 0.2 m/s, the Space Shuttle's approach rule. Sideways offsets are steered out at 1/100 of the offset per second. The corridor takes about 1,850 s.

facts.title: The ±10° approach corridor cone
facts.text: The docking approach corridor is a cone of ±10° around the docking axis, reaching back from the station's aft port. facts.title: Keep-out sphere and keep-in sphere
facts.text: The station's keep-out sphere (KOS) has a 200 m radius around its centre of mass; the docking ship may enter it only through the approach corridor after GO, and being inside it anywhere else in a normal phase fails the run as a 'KOS violation'. A 3 km keep-in sphere also bounds the scenario: leaving it fails the run as 'keep-in exit'.

facts.title: The 3 m commit check
facts.text: At 3 m from the port the docking autopilot makes a final commit check: lateral offset at most 8 cm, attitude error at most 3° and body rates at most 0.15°/s. If any fails it breaks out ('IDSS gate at the 3 m commit'); once committed, no further abort checks run before contact.

facts.title: What IDSS stands for
facts.text: IDSS is the International Docking System Standard, a common docking-interface standard agreed by the International Space Station partner agencies so that different vehicles can dock to the same ports. Astro Pilot's docking scenario judges each contact against IDSS-style limits on speed, alignment and rotation rate.

facts.title: Passive safety (Rule P)
facts.text: Passive safety means that if every jet failed right after a burn, the ship would still drift clear of the station. Astro Pilot's docking scenario enforces this as 'Rule P' after the departure burn, each mid-course correction and every breakout, checking 24 hours of free drift, sampled every 60 s (10 s for breakouts), against the worst constant drag within the bound.

facts.title: Rule P distances and margin
facts.text: For the docking transfer, Rule P requires the 24-hour free drift after the departure burn and each mid-course correction to stay at least 240 m from the station's centre. The planner aims for 248 m, an 8 m margin, since in its Monte Carlo flown states landed up to 5 m below plan. If the true drift breaks Rule P, the run fails ('Rule P after DEPART' or 'after MCC').

facts.title: Rule A: always keep an escape
facts.text: Holds on V-bar and the approach corridor are not passively safe: per the docking design's analysis, drag would carry a ship parked at H1 into the station in about 8 hours. facts.title: Differential drag in the docking scenario
facts.text: Each docking run draws one constant differential drag between ship and station, uniform within ±2e-7 m/s² along-track, which the design puts at about 30 % of the ISS's drag. At the negative extreme the ship sinks and moves ahead: after 24 hours of free drift it would be about 2.2 km forward and 31 m lower.

facts.title: What triggers a docking breakout
facts.text: A docking breakout is triggered by NO-GO at H1 or H2 lasting over 1,800 s, navigation placing the ship outside the corridor cone inside the keep-out sphere, a failed 3 m commit check, no available passively safe escape (Rule A), or a failed sideways-translation jet. If the escape ends passively safe, the report card reads 'Breakout' and names the abort reason.

facts.title: How a breakout ends
facts.text: Breakout burns in the docking scenario are pre-validated before they fly, so they bypass the safety filter, as real collision-avoidance burns do, and each bypass is logged. After the burn the phase is DEPART, and the run ends as a breakout once the ship is over 210 m from the station, provided the true drift passed the breakout check after the burn.

facts.text: In the docking design's verification, a breakout started 3–30 m from the port while closing at 0.10 m/s, or 100 m out at 0.2 m/s, moves only 0.97–1.15 m further forward, exits the keep-out sphere in 760–1,160 s, never re-enters within 24 hours, next passes no closer than 367 m, and costs 0.13–0.21 m/s.

facts.title: LVLH frame, V-bar and R-bar
facts.text: The docking scenario works in the station's LVLH frame, in metres: X points along-track in the direction of orbital motion (V-bar), Y points radially up away from Earth (R-bar is the radial line toward Earth), and Z is cross-track. The origin is the station's centre of mass, and the ship approaches from behind, along V-bar.

facts.title: Clohessy–Wiltshire relative motion
facts.text: Relative motion in Astro Pilot's docking scenario follows the Clohessy–Wiltshire (Hill) equations, published in 1960 for rendezvous guidance: X'' = −2n Y' + aX + ad, Y'' = 3n² Y + 2n X' + aY, Z'' = −n² Z + aZ, where n is the orbital rate, a the jets' acceleration and ad differential drag. They describe linearised motion near a circular orbit.

facts.title: The station's orbit in docking
facts.text: The docking scenario's station flies a circular orbit 420 km up, with orbital rate n = 1.128e-3 rad/s and a period of 5,569 s (92.8 minutes). Holding attitude in the rotating LVLH frame therefore means turning at 0.0646°/s relative to the stars.

facts.title: Exact integration of the relative motion
facts.text: Astro Pilot's docking simulation integrates translation exactly with the Clohessy–Wiltshire state-transition matrix, thrust held constant over each step, so position errors do not build up. Steps are 10 ms in any 100 ms cycle where a jet fires or the ship rotates faster than 0.2°/s, otherwise 100 ms.

facts.title: Rigid-body attitude of the docking ship
facts.text: The docking ship's attitude is simulated as a full rigid body: Euler's equations with jet torques and gravity-gradient torque, quaternion kinematics relative to the rotating LVLH frame, and 4th-order Runge–Kutta integration renormalised every step. The inertia is 1.715, 11.74 and 11.35 million kg·m² about roll, yaw and pitch.

facts.title: Minimum impulse bit and jet timing
facts.text: A jet's minimum impulse bit (MIB) is its shortest reliable pulse. Astro Pilot's docking jets are timed in 10 ms steps within 100 ms cycles; a request shorter than the MIB is not fired but carried to the next cycle. One 40 ms primary pulse gives 154.8 N·s, 1.63 mm/s for the 95 t ship.

facts.title: Translation jet pairs
facts.text: Two primary jets push the 95 t docking ship at about 0.0815 m/s², the intro card's 'about 0.08 m/s²'. Fixed pairs translate it: P13+P14 at the tail push forward (+X), P15+P16 at the nose brake (−X), P2+P4 push up, P1+P3 push down, and P6+P8 or P5+P7 push sideways.

facts.title: How attitude jets are chosen
facts.text: Attitude torques on the docking ship come from primaries P1–P12 or verniers V1–V6, chosen every 100 ms by bounded least squares: each jet between off and full-on, minimising torque error plus a fuel penalty weighted by mass flow (1.409 kg/s per primary, 0.041 kg/s per vernier). Cross-torques from translation jets are fed forward.

facts.title: Flight rule for failed lateral jets
facts.text: The docking autopilot obeys a flight rule: no entry into the keep-out sphere without torque-balanced sideways translation. If any lateral translation primary P1–P8 has failed, the run breaks out with 'NO-GO: a lateral translation jet has failed': a far start still flies the transfer and aborts at H1 (a failed P1 aborts before departure), and a final start aborts at H2.

facts.title: Why a failed P1 aborts at the start
facts.text: A failed P1 jet makes a far-start docking run break out before the transfer: the departure is a downward radial burn, and P1 is the only downward-pushing primary at the nose, so the burn would fly lopsided for 155–276 s and miss passive safety. A failed P3 is covered by the aft P9/P11 pair (a 5–17 s burn), and the transfer flies.

facts.title: Control with an unbalanced jet pair
facts.text: When a failed jet leaves a sideways translation pair unbalanced, Astro Pilot's docking control switches those cycles to one joint six-degree-of-freedom jet selection over the working attitude jets plus the translation jets for the needed directions, solving force and torque together with torque weighted first. A lone forward or braking jet on the X axis stays on its fixed path, its torque fed forward.

facts.title: The docking safety filter
facts.text: Every docking guidance velocity command except a breakout burn passes a safety filter once a second that projects it onto the nearest safe velocity with Dykstra's method. facts.title: Attitude control modes
facts.text: The docking autopilot's phase-plane attitude control has two modes, shown on the HUD: primary (deadband 1°, rates up to 0.5°/s) for burns, breakouts included, and vernier (rates up to 0.05°/s) otherwise, with a 1° deadband in the transfer coast, 0.3° in holds and the corridor, and 0.1° in FINAL. facts.title: Translation control law
facts.text: Docking translation control commands the acceleration (v_des − v)/τ minus the natural Clohessy–Wiltshire acceleration, with τ = 5 s (2 s in FINAL) and a 5 mm/s deadband (4 mm/s along the axis in FINAL); it keeps firing until the error falls to 40 % of the deadband. Burns fly as closed-loop trims until within 1.2 mm/s along X and 0.5 mm/s on Y and Z.

facts.title: r versus rho on the HUD
facts.text: In the docking HUD, r is the distance between the ship's and the station's centres of mass, and rho is the distance between the two docking ports; on V-bar, rho ≈ r − 32.8 m. So H1 (r = 250 m) is rho ≈ 217 m, H2 is rho = 20 m, and capture happens at r ≈ 32.8 m.

facts.title: How it follows NASA practice
facts.text: Astro Pilot's docking scenario copies NASA proximity-operations practice: a keep-out sphere entered only through an approach corridor after GO/NO-GO checks at hold points, passive safety after transfer burns and breakouts, the Space Shuttle's approach-speed rule, and a pre-planned breakout. The code is Astro Pilot's own JavaScript, not NASA flight software.

facts.title: Manual flight keys
facts.text: Astro Pilot's manual flight keys: W or Up arrow pitches the nose up, S or Down arrow pitches it down, A or Left arrow yaws left, D or Right arrow yaws right, Q rolls left, E rolls right, Shift boosts and X or Ctrl brakes. The keys command turn rates, and fly-by-wire keeps the ship moving where its nose points.

facts.title: Edge guard and tunnel guide in manual
facts.text: Astro Pilot's corridor is 36 units wide with invisible edges (in space also a ceiling and a floor). facts.title: How fast browser training runs
facts.text: In-browser PPO training in Astro Pilot reaches about 6,000 environment steps per second on an Apple M3 Pro laptop; slower machines show fewer in the Steps / s tile. Training uses TensorFlow.js on its WebGL backend and falls back to the CPU backend when WebGL is unavailable.

facts.title: Earth zoom offline and known limits

facts.title: Landing uses classical control, not RL
facts.text: No neural network or reinforcement learning flies the Astro Pilot landing. The autoland is a classical, model-based guidance, navigation and control (GNC) stack like the autopilots of certified CAT III airliners; the AI part is CMA-ES, an evolutionary optimizer that tuned about two dozen of its gains and thresholds offline. The PPO reinforcement-learning pilot belongs to the corridor game.

facts.title: Why the landing does not use RL
facts.text: The Astro Pilot landing design chose tuned classical GNC over a deep-RL policy because end-to-end RL (PPO or SAC) matches but rarely beats tuned GNC, has poor worst cases, is opaque and needs millions of episodes. A model-based autoland stays interpretable and certifiable, and CMA-ES tuning still optimizes it against bad-weather tails. An RL comparison is left as future work.

facts.title: Delta-wing lift and ground effect
facts.text: The Astro Pilot landing spaceplane's lift uses the Polhamus delta-wing model: potential lift plus vortex lift from the leading-edge vortices, protected at 20° angle of attack. Ground effect raises lift (about 10% at touchdown height) and cuts induced drag as the wing nears the runway, which the flare has to handle.

facts.title: Landing gear of the spaceplane

facts.title: What CMA-ES is
facts.text: CMA-ES (Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy, by Hansen) is an evolutionary optimizer: each generation it samples candidate parameter sets from a Gaussian, ranks them, and shifts and reshapes the Gaussian toward the best. It needs no gradients, so it can tune a controller just by flying simulations. Astro Pilot used CMA-ES to tune its landing autoland.

facts.text: The Astro Pilot autoland's roughly two dozen gains and thresholds were tuned offline by CMA-ES with 14 candidates per generation; each candidate flew 80 seeded final approaches in randomly drawn weather. facts.title: Circular Kepler orbit formulas
facts.text: Astro Pilot's Earth orbit is a circular Kepler orbit: speed = √(μ/a) and period = 2π√(a³/μ), where a is the Earth's radius plus the altitude. At 420 km that gives 7.66 km/s and 92.8 minutes.

facts.text: Astro Pilot is a browser demo in which a spacecraft in Earth orbit learns to fly through an asteroid field with comets streaking through it. The pilot is a small neural network trained with proximal policy optimisation (PPO) in TensorFlow.js, and the 3D scene is drawn with three.js.

facts.title: How the pilot learned
facts.text: The Astro Pilot pilot learned by trial and error (reinforcement learning): it earned reward for progressing east (up to cruise speed) with its nose east and wings level, lost a little for jerky or wasteful control and for flying close to rocks or walls, and lost 20 points on any crash. PPO adjusted its network to collect more reward.

facts.title: The pilot's neural network
facts.text: The Astro Pilot pilot is a small neural network: separate actor and critic networks, each with two hidden layers of 128 tanh units, trained with PPO-Clip. facts.text: The Astro Pilot spacecraft flies with moving control surfaces: four elevons, split rudders on two canted fins that also open as a Shuttle-style speed brake, a body flap, and exhaust plumes that vector up to 6°. facts.title: The procedural asteroids
facts.text: The Astro Pilot asteroids are procedural: noise-displaced spheres with 3–8 craters, some shaped like contact binaries (like Itokawa) or spinning tops (like Bennu), tinted by real albedo classes. Their sizes follow a collisional power law, and they drift west at 2–7 units per second with smooth random wander, spin, and bounce off each other.

facts.title: How fast browser training is
facts.text: In-browser training in Astro Pilot runs 128 environments × 64 steps per PPO update with minibatches of 2048, reaching about 6,000 environment steps per second on an Apple M3 Pro. TensorFlow.js is limited by per-operation overhead, so a few large minibatches are what make browser training fast.

facts.title: The dodging is learned, not scripted

facts.title: A Gaussian policy squashed by tanh
facts.text: The Astro Pilot actor is a Gaussian policy: the network outputs the mean of each action and a learned, state-independent log standard deviation sets the spread. The environment squashes every action with tanh into the range -1 to 1.

facts.title: Exploration noise limits (log-std)
facts.text: The Astro Pilot policy's log standard deviation starts at -0.7 and is clipped to between -2.5 and 0.5 after every update. The floor of -2.5 keeps a minimum of exploration noise (a standard deviation of about 0.08 before tanh), so training can never make the policy fully deterministic.

facts.title: What a sensor beam value means

PPO improves the policy in small, safe steps by clipping each update so the new policy cannot move too far from the old one; Astro Pilot trains its pilot with PPO in TensorFlow.js.

facts.text: The sim-to-real gap is the difference between a simulator and the real world that can make a policy trained in simulation fail on real hardware. facts.title: What a language model does
facts.text: A language model generates text one token at a time, each time predicting a likely next token from everything before it. A token is a word or a piece of a word; in English one token averages about three-quarters of a word.

facts.title: Pilot Eye runtime: WASM worker, 6 MB
facts.text: Pilot Eye runs in a background Web Worker with onnxruntime-web 1.30 on WebAssembly, using one thread, so the game's main thread keeps its frame rate. facts.title: Pilot Eye architecture: MobileNetV4
facts.text: Pilot Eye is a multi-task convolutional network: a pretrained MobileNetV4-Conv-Small backbone (from timm, Apache-2.0) turns each 160×96 frame into a 64-channel 3×5 feature map. A small head pools the newest map and its differences from the two earlier frames' maps, adds the two frame spacings and passes them through a 512-unit layer to predict all outputs at once.

facts.title: Pilot Eye advice actions
facts.text: Pilot Eye's advice is one of CONTINUE, CLIMB, DESCEND, TURN_LEFT, TURN_RIGHT, SPEED_UP, SLOW_DOWN, GO_AROUND, HOLD_POSITION, BREAKOUT or NONE_SAFE, limited per scene: the corridors use the first seven, landing adds GO_AROUND, and docking uses CONTINUE, BREAKOUT, HOLD_POSITION and SLOW_DOWN. facts.title: Pilot Eye reason codes
facts.text: Pilot Eye's 26 reasons cover hazards and terrain (hazard ahead, closing fast, terrain or buildings close, corridor edge), the flight envelope and weather (stall, overstress, severe turbulence, storm cell, pull up), the approach and runway (unstable approach, localizer or glideslope deviation, speed, sink rate, crosswind, tailwind, runway edge, cannot stop) and docking (keep-out sphere, closing too fast, misalignment, attitude, jet failure, low propellant, no breakout).

facts.title: What Pilot Eye cannot see
facts.text: Pilot Eye's training labels leave out rules that 160×96 pixels cannot show, such as low propellant, failed jets, breakout availability, tailwind, some approach, runway, turbulence and attitude-rate rules, docking closing-speed rules beyond 11 m, all glideslope-dot rules and localizer-dot rules farther than 1 NM from the runway. The full labels reached the Narrator's training through its text and Context line.

facts.title: Five scene families
facts.text: Astro Pilot Vision sorts frames into five scene families: S, the deep-space corridor through the asteroid belt; A, the atmospheric corridor over routes such as the Alps or cities; L, the airliner landing approach; D, rendezvous and docking; and Z, Earth-zoom telescope views. Each family has its own label rules, frame spacing and allowed actions.

facts.title: Why two models instead of one
facts.text: Astro Pilot uses two vision models instead of one because the fastest small vision-language models measured about 190–256 ms to their first token, roughly 20 times over a per-frame budget, and a generative model can hallucinate a safety verdict. A small CNN with fixed output heads can judge every frame and be calibrated, while the Narrator explains on demand.

facts.title: Narrator vision encoder: own 8-bit build
facts.text: The Narrator's vision encoder is the project's own weight-only 8-bit re-quantisation of the published fp32 SmolVLM encoder: 109.8 MB, about 279 ms per image on WebGPU, with 0.9997 cosine similarity to full precision. facts.title: Deterministic capture in headless Chromium

facts.title: Corridor safety labels by replay
facts.text: Corridor safety labels come from simulated what-ifs: from each labelled moment the simulator replays 3 seconds (45 steps) four times for each of seven manoeuvres. Unsafe means hands-off flight crashes in at least half the replays, or the ship is stalled, overstressed or about to hit the ground. Caution means fewer crashes, a median hands-off clearance of 2.5 units (about 48 m) or less, or severe turbulence.

facts.text: The corridor's "nothing changes" reference is HANDS_OFF (neutral stick, throttle held), not the learned atmospheric pilot, which cannot see radar or air data and crashes 25–46 times a minute in the Alps. facts.title: Landing safety labels
facts.text: Astro Pilot Vision landing labels follow the autoland: a frame is Unsafe if the continued approach ends in a crash, runway excursion, overrun, short landing, tailstrike or hard landing, or if the approach is not stabilized at 500 ft. It is Caution on a go-around, an unstable approach between 1000 and 500 ft, a crosswind of 15 kt or more, a tailwind of 10 kt or more, or severe turbulence.

facts.title: Docking safety labels
facts.text: Astro Pilot Vision docking labels follow the GNC autopilot: a frame is Unsafe if the run ends in a failed contact or keep-out-sphere violation, or the ship closes faster than 1.5 times the axial speed limit inside 20 m. It is Caution on a breakout, an attitude error over 2°, a rate over 0.1°/s, propellant under 40 %, a failed jet or closing above the limit.

facts.title: Fault injection for dangerous examples
facts.text: To get enough dangerous examples without breaking the simulators, faults were injected into 35 % of landing and docking episodes, 25 % of deep-space and 10 % of atmospheric ones. facts.text: About 10 % of the Astro Pilot Vision question-answer pairs are trick questions with a false premise, such as asking about an airliner that is not there, a wrong distance ("We are 50 m from the station, right?") or a wrong place ("Is this Tokyo?"). facts.title: How Earth views were chosen
facts.text: The Astro Pilot Vision Earth-zoom views come from 200 locations × 4 views: 35 % cities of 50,000+ people, 20 % peaks, 15 % named regions such as deserts or deltas, 20 % random land and 10 % coast or ocean. Range was drawn log-uniformly up to 2,500 km, tilt up to 60°, the Sun from 18° below to 70° above the horizon, and 30 % were lit "Always day".

facts.text: Place names in Astro Pilot Vision Earth-zoom captions come from Natural Earth (public domain, version 5.1.2): cities, countries, regions, peaks, lakes, rivers and glaciers, located on the frame with the captured camera. facts.title: Pilot Eye quality gates
facts.text: Pilot Eye's quality gates ask for a mean within-family Unsafe-vs-rest AUROC (0.5 is chance, 1.0 perfect) of at least 0.75, a pooled AUROC of at least 0.80 that beats a scene-and-conditions-only baseline by 0.10, and a higher Unsafe probability in at least 80 % of frame pairs differing only by an injected fault. The v0 Pilot Eye on the site is still below these gates.

facts.title: Sim-to-real gap: not for real flight
facts.text: The Astro Pilot vision models' training used only simulator frames, so there is a sim-to-real gap: they are not validated on real camera images and must not be used for real flight, landing or docking decisions. facts.title: Designed fallbacks not shipped

facts.title: Why the thin-air ceiling exists

facts.text: Astro Pilot's aero coefficients were tuned to unit-tested design targets: level flight at cruise near a density ratio of 0.8 needs about 35–60 % throttle, full power climbs about 3 units/s at cruise, and a 60°-bank, 2-g turn at cruise has a radius of about 12 units.

facts.title: Why cumulus are bumpy
facts.text: Real cumulus clouds sit atop rising thermals, and their flat bases form at the height where rising air cools to its dew point and condenses. Air rises under and inside them and sinks around them, which is why flying near cumulus is bumpy, in Astro Pilot as in reality.

facts.title: Gust length scales
facts.text: Astro Pilot's Dryden length scales follow the low-altitude model with 1 unit = 19 m = 62.3 ft: the vertical scale L_w equals the height h above ground and L_u = L_v = h/(0.177 + 0.000823h)^1.2 (h in feet), becoming isotropic above about 2,000 ft; inside a cloud its own scale, 0.4 × radius, takes over in proportion to the cloud's share.

facts.title: Why clouds glow at the edges
facts.text: Clouds glow at their edges when backlit because water droplets scatter light strongly forward (Mie scattering), while light is dimmed exponentially with depth (the Beer–Lambert law). facts.title: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck random wander

facts.title: Comet dust tail physics
facts.text: Astro Pilot's comet dust tail is simulated: each particle is born at the nucleus with a small launch toward the Sun, then radiation pressure pushes it away from the Sun at 3.2 units/s^2 while the nucleus flies on, so the dust tail curves behind the comet. Each dust particle lives 2.6 seconds, and its motion is integrated in the vertex shader.
